title: Getting to Zero
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: The main teaching of the Soto Zen dharma talk emphasizes the importance of cultivating a sense of aspiration or longing for spiritual growth through mindfulness and dedication to practice. This involves setting aside distractions and being present in all aspects of life, including daily tasks, by embracing a "zero" state where there is no preconceived notion or attachment. By doing so, individuals can tap into their true nature, experience life fully and authentically, and find peace and harmony within themselves and with others.

sentences.text: Everyone, give me just a second here.
Hi everyone out in Zoom Zendo.
Well, this talk has continued to evolve.
Can you hear me okay, Terry?
Yeah, Hannah?
Great.
Everyone over there and everyone out there, this talk has continued to evolve and we'll see where it turns.
I was really touched to remember that at Red Cedar and Everyday Zen, when you open a lecture, actually everyone bows together.
It's not just the person giving the lecture.
So we do bring out the Dharma together.
The title of this talk is something like Getting to Zero.
First, I just want to say how touched I am to be back here at Red Cedar.
I think this is something like the 33rd year that Red Cedar has existed, in the 20-some practice periods that you have had.

The continuous heartfelt practice here, through all kinds of changes and through COVID and having to move and finding a building and putting forth the energy again and again and again, is really inspiring and very moving.
It's a small core with a big heart, of many people coming and participating.
I also want to give gratitude to Noman for inviting me to come and share this practice period with you, and with Ikushen Desiree.
For those of you who don't know, I practiced at Red Cedar for about three and a half years, and Desiree and I came to know each other during that time.
So I'm thrilled that she has been given the opportunity to be Shusou, thinking that she is a very ripe plum on the branch, picked to help lead this practice period.
And she'll tell you more tomorrow.
There's no microphone.
Yeah, so I'll just try and speak up, and feel free to move in a little bit.
I don't know if you do that in this space, but feel free to move in a little bit if you can't hear me.
Ikushen will tell you a little bit more about herself tomorrow, in her Way Seeking Mind Talk.

But in the context of what I'm trying to do today, which is to provide a little bit of fuel for the six or eight weeks of practice period here, I want to say Ikushen started in practice over 30 years ago in Colorado and practiced much of her early years with Nat Han and went to Plum Village.

In fact, there's a very touching picture of her and her then very young son Luke with [unclear: "Tai"] together, that says something about the continuity of Ikushen's, of Desiree's, life and involvement with practice.

When she came here to the Pacific Northwest, for some years she made the trek from Mount Vernon after work up to Mountain Lamp to be able to practice, and practice in their sesshins, and she's done the same for the last seven or eight years here.
So really, an enormous commitment and a light to practice the Dharma, and so she's a very apt student to be Shusou.
This is a wonderful example for us and a mirror of what all of us have done to get here.

There's not a person here in this room who didn't need to make some adjustments to their life schedule, to their commitments, to ask for the flexibility of their families and the support of their families in order to arrive at the sesshin, and also to put forward the additional effort that you are making in order to participate in the practice period overall.
So although the Shusou steps forward and is the shining example to us all, actually she's a mirror to you, and you help support her and she helps support you.
So what is the role of the Shusou during practice period?

A number of former Shusous are here, but I'll just say for those of you who don't know, pragmatically we say it's to share the teaching seat, and indeed she'll give, I think, two lectures, formal lectures, in front of us all.

One tomorrow, talking about how she arrived at practice and what that Way Seeking Mind is, and one is a culmination of her understanding, just in time for the Dharma, bringing out the Dharma together in the Shusou Hosein ceremony.
And as you all know, the Shusou here at Red Cedar does a class.
I'm really heartened that Desiree has chosen her core teacher's teachings and really basic Buddhism, and is willing to dig in from the experience of her own life.
I think that's what practice is all about for all of us: to turn towards how practice speaks to us and how it manifests in our own life.
As she's presenting the class material, our work is to take that material and examine it through the lens of our own lives.
So that's the bare bones of what the Shusou does.
But actually the Shusou is so much more than that.

More importantly, the Shusou functions to express something of the Dharma in terms of how she embodies the Dharma, showing us how the Dharma is expressed not in words but out of our body and in our life.
The Shusou embodies the continuous practice of.
So you're under the magnifying glass as an example.
I'll talk more about what continuous practice is at the end of the talk, but I just want to hold that up.

Really, there's an energy, and we each have a different way of being, but in practice there's a kind of joy that manifests when we come into that groove of being in our life, a kind of wholehearted "I've found it, I've arrived, I'm here."
You can sense that, I think, in the practice of someone who's been settled for a while, even through the ups and downs.
We're still a kind of steady core.
I think that's what we see in people who really inspire us, and I think that's what you'll find when you look around and look to the example of our Shusou.
The thing is, we all have that potentiality within ourselves, and so that example touches something within us, something that we can find for ourselves.
I really appreciate that in the practice here, for practice period, we talk less and we sit zazen more.
So the weekday sitting programs are not a lecture but actually more zazen.

Zazen is really the heart of our practice and the heart of finding our way to this kind of continuous practice, this way of being fully present in the moment, this way of connecting with that inner core that we have.
I think it's part of the Shusou's role to sit every period, and I'd encourage you to do your best to sit every period of zazen with her, to the extent that your life and your schedule will allow.
Our practice, the understanding of what our practice is, and a realization of an awakened life really arise out of the physicality of our practice.
It took me many, many years to really get that in my body, how core it is.

This ability to attend moment to moment to moment arises out of the fine attunement that we have, when we sit, to our mental and our physical states of mind, and to find a stability within the midst of it, being formed by the information that comes and arises in our body moment to moment, no matter what our circumstances are.
That really becomes accessible in a conscious way, in a way in which we have, I'm sorry, does anyone else not hear me?
Come.
Thank you.
We have all kinds of unconscious things going on in our minds, and we act out of them.
As someone who struggled with impulsivity, and still does, that kind of unconsciousness really resides in the body.
The more we sit and we settle, the more accessible those workings are, and the more choice we have, as we'll review when we study the first noble truth and the second noble truth.
Really overcoming or coming to terms with those has to do with having choice, and that choice, in my experience, arises from becoming intimate and settled with whatever arises in the body.
So zazen is good in practice and in practice period.
Maybe I'll confess first: I look back at my old teacher's beginning-of-practice-period talks and writings, and so I'm weaving together some of his ideas with my own flavor.
In practice period there's always a balance of inspiration and aspiration.
Inspiration is usually what we think of as the [unclear: "shoe"], as I've been talking about.
And the teacher, Uchiyama Roshi, says the teacher is the engine for practice.
The teacher's constancy, the teacher's virya, energy, the teacher's effort really, and the teacher's ease and joy are part of what inspire us and let us know what practice can be.

Noman and John and a few others have been a constant presence for 30 years here, showing up, pulling out the zabutons, taking care of all the details that evolved over time, balancing the books, buying the food, schlepping the whatever.
That kind of constancy, with a lightness and a care and an inclusiveness, is an inspiration that touches something in us.
It awakens an interest in practice and a joy in practice.
It's an inspiring example, and it also encourages us in what might be possible.
And that's where the aspiration comes from.
The teacher and the [unclear: "shoe so"] are the engine, but we don't just follow along like cars on the train.
We bring our own [unclear: "kiddling"] and our own logs to stoke the fire, and we support each other in doing that.
So we feel the settledness, we touch that in ourselves, we recognize that in ourselves, and that supports each other.
That's why it's so valuable and helpful to each other that we come and we practice together.
Aspiration is what we long for or what we hope for.
It's that which you are seeking.
That which you are seeking is causing you to seek it.
It's already within you.
It is what Suzuki Roshi called the inmost request.
I like to call it the yearning.
There's something about that word that really speaks to a longing to reconnect and be whole.
That's our aspiration.
It's so much bigger than our normal, mundane things that we want for ourselves.
It comes from a deeper place than the wish for material things.
Perhaps for you it's a peace of mind, to be kind, to be helpful, to be present.
I think these things arise in part, or can be helped, by seeing an example.
For me, probably the strongest was Okumura Roshi.
I had the chance to practice with him for many practice periods, and even on Zoom, his gentleness and humility and clarity are an inspiration.
You really get a sense that he doesn't want anything for himself and that he functions as a vehicle of practice.
That's pretty inspiring.

He said of his first teacher, he had read a book by his first teacher, and he said of his first teacher after reading his book, he'd all but dropped out of high school at that point, he said, "I want to be like him.
I want to be like him."
There's something in us that wants to be our best self.
We want to be whole.
It's a shorthand for "there's something you have touched that emanates, that I would personally like to understand and be like.
I want to be like that."
We all have our best selves inside.

When we're free from the three poisons of greed, hate and delusion, our own true nature comes forth: our intention not to cause harm, to do good, to gather the way, to be of benefit for all beings, the three pure precepts.
That's all inside of ourselves, and sometimes we can see it, and that helps us remember how to touch it.
So I really like to encourage a practice, not just for practice period but a practice overall, to help cultivate our aspiration, to help us be in touch with that aspiration.
That is, to name it in some way and then to plant it in your zazen.
So at a period of zazen, just to raise, just like Dogen talks about raising the thought of enlightenment, raise the thought of what your inmost request is.
What is that yearning?
Not to figure out a way of how to get there, but actually just, in a way, it's like offering up a prayer or offering up your life: "Just like this, this is the direction I want to go."
You could put it in your phone and tell Siri, "How do I get to," but it's not like that.
You put it in your zazen and just offer it up.
Sometimes, kind of miraculously, the instructions appear after months or years, without you knowing.
"May I be kind.
May I be present.
May I treat others with respect.
May I have curiosity.
How do I follow this path?
How do I live with this terrible loneliness and still practice the Dharma?"
Just offer it up.

And actually, for what it's worth, there's neuroscience that says that this calling forth invites our subconscious to include it in its awareness as we go about our day, and as we sleep we might also touch on it at different points of the day.
There was a time in my early years of practice when I was working in a busy emergency department, and every day people had a lot of stuff going on.
It was an urban emergency department.
Every day, before I'd pick up a chart and go into the patient's room, knock on the door and go in, I would evoke my intention to be kind, to be present, [unclear: "to show off"].

Whether you're driving to work and can sit in your car for 15 seconds to breathe and bring that intention, before you pick up your daughter from preschool, or while you stand in the grocery line, whatever it is, periodically throughout the day you can keep that thought alive.
So what is practice period?
What are we doing here?
Ango is the Japanese word Master Dogen, the founder of our lineage, used.
It means peaceful and harmonious abiding for all things.
How to find peace: peace within my mind, peace within my body and mind, and with each other.
Like in sesshin, we gather our heart and place it 100 percent within the container of practice with each other.
I think that's what practice period is: gather our heart and place it 100 percent with each other.
And last night, my goodness, last night was such a beautiful example of that.

Perhaps it's been a while since Red Cedar has had so many people come at the beginning of a practice period, and everyone, even people here for the first time, offered themselves up out of the container of this practice being held by Everyone.
I also really appreciate that at Red Cedar the practice period is at the first of the year.
It's a really wonderful time of year.
We've generally just been through a relatively quiet time.

I know holidays aren't quiet in some ways, but in other ways, with the very short days that we have up here and the slowing down of certain kinds of activities, it's a time to be a little more contemplative or relational with people that we care about.
There's a chance to settle, go a little deeper and think about what matters.
Sometimes we make New Year's resolutions.
They can be helpful, but as we know they're often based on mundane aspects of how to spend our time and on personal goals: I want to do this, I want to be thinner, 20 pounds.
I want to start an exercise program, I'd like to learn a language, whatever it is.
All worthy, but not based on very much that's deep.

So the majority of them are forgotten within the first months of the year, or they get pushed out of the way by some other new shiny idea or the pressing problems of life, unless they're a very fundamental part of our values.
They drop by the wayside of the pressures and routines of our lives.
Those intentions aren't rooted in the real fabric of what's important to us, but more in what we want or think we should do, so our motivation doesn't have the staying power.
In practice period we look to go deeper, to find that place of what's really important to me.
What is my deepest intention here?
What do I hope for in my life, in my practice?
Now, my old teacher Sojun Mel Weitsman of the Berkeley Zen Center used to say that practice period was resetting our lives to zero, clearing the slate and getting back to basics.
That's a real invitation to think about how you live your life now, and what kinds of things you're pulling back to after the holidays, and what kinds of things you get busy with.

Whether they're the projects you have going, the relationships that maybe aren't so important for nurturing, the kinds of tasks you do and how you structure them, how you spend your precious time: clearing the slate, and what you want to write on it during practice period is a wonderful thing to examine.

Actually, practice period invites all of us to ask: what small things can I set aside during this time to allow myself to attend the class, do the workshop, or put more attention to zazen, to the workings of practice maybe?
Try not to add anything in too fast in this new year.
Set aside any commitments or activities that you routinely do, so that you can allow space for the unknown to manifest itself, and to the activities that you do, bring your whole practice.
A clear mind is quiet and not cluttered with ideas that can control us and distract us from what's important to us.
I don't know about you all, but I certainly am aware of the way in which media comes flying at us, the [unclear: "next messages"] that come in moment after moment.
We've all developed, generically in society, maybe not you, but I'll speak for myself, the habit of feeling like I need to respond now.
I certainly notice when I haven't responded in an hour and I get another text that other people have that feeling too.
Can we slow down?
Can we say maybe only do this once a day?
It depends on your life, of course.
Three times a day, once a week: can I check these messages, can I respond, can I pay more attention to how my time is being used?
As Master Dogen says, to use the 24 hours instead of being used by the 24 hours.
It's like actually being conscious about using the time.
Any idea, I can look up the weather by the hour: the atmospheric rivers these last couple of weeks, the wettest day, where is it, how many inches, and when was the record.
All of that is very interesting, but it's a seductive distraction from what's important.
How do you really want to spend your time?
What's really important to you?
Buddha's words on right speech came to me when I think about this engagement with all the stimulation.
It might be interesting, but is it helpful?
Is it really helpful?
Is it really necessary?
Is it really timely?
Do I have to do it right now?
Those are really important questions to be asking when you want to make the best use of your time, and also, if you will, to train your mind.
A lot of practice is mind training, learning to not be unconscious about what we do but to be conscious in our choices, and so to have freedom in our choices.
It almost seems counterintuitive, like freedom is I can get on my phone anytime I want and do anything I want, but actually the phone's in charge of me these days.
Oftentimes the real freedom is in saying, this is what's important to me, this is when I need to do it, these are the other aspects of your life.
So we experience getting to zero through zazen.
That's how we have, I think, come to know physically in our body, when we sit in a stable posture and just pay attention to what's very present, not caught chasing after anything.
This is the hardest and the simplest thing in the world.
Those moments of being fully present are like being at zero.

There's nothing pulling in the one direction, there's nothing pushing from the other direction, and the experience of the senses is fresh and alive like the first time, because there's nothing before and there's nothing after.
It's just what it is, right in this moment.
When we're at zero there's no inside or outside.
There's nothing excluded, everything's included, a certain way.
Nothing's included, either, because it's all there.
There's no inner, outside, it's just what it is in that moment.
I think this is such a helpful experience in zazen, because when you get off the cushion you [unclear: "wear zero"] off the cushion.
Immediately there are choices, and a person who's there, and ideas about things.
We usually think about our life as being either inside the gate or outside the gate.
Inside is when you log into the Zoom zendo or when you come here to sit together, and outside is everything else.
There's a tendency to think about our practice kind of like the Sunday church of when we show up, even if that includes the periods of zazen.
But actually our practice is always continuous with time, and more and more with zazen, gradually, the essence of zazen is presence in everything we do.
Because, again, you have it in your body, that feeling of being in the breath, in the body.
Zazen is doing zazen within you, and so moving in the world it's much easier to find that place of being at zero.
That means receiving the circumstances as they are, without a lot of preconceived ideas of the self, of who you are and what you want in each moment.
Clearing the decks for all but the essential, for a time, supports the experience of integrating practice into our lives.
It's like wiping the windshield or lifting the weight off our backs for a while, and freeing our energy to pay attention, to actually experience what it's like to be in the present moment.
As usual I don't have a good sense of time for these, so let me say a little bit more about this quality of continuous practice.
I've just said that zazen is a way of physically experiencing each moment after moment.
Sometimes it's said "just this."
In a way the "just" is extra.
It's taking a step back from our usual ways of thinking and allowing what, with curiosity, not knowing, just receiving what, moment after moment.

I think that is the heart of zazen, with an open hand in your experiences: what's this, what now, what now. [unclear: "editing a quality of that"] a quality of continuous practice is what we sometimes call mindfulness.
It's showing up with full body presence to what's in front of ourselves.
I think Sojin Roshi, emulating his teacher Suzuki Roshi, was really a master of it.
The practice was really about whatever came up, being fully present with whoever it was, and finding great joy and creating together.

Moving the rocks at Tassajara and cooking in the kitchen together were examples of that, just with a lightness, not coming from having an idea of what needs to be done but not having an idea of how it will happen, allowing that to be co-created.
The relationship, the creation, mattered more than the actual doing of it.
It's kind of like saying allowing things to manifest themselves, and not trying to grab a hold of them and make them do what you want them to.
To do that with each moment, with people, that is the art of continuous practice when we get off the cushion and move.
That may be as much as kind of fits right now.
At the beginning of one of the first practice periods at Tassajara Zen Monastery, Suzuki Roshi started the practice period by saying this:
*Real luminous happiness is not at all obtained by the removal of every difficulty.
If it were, it would be a bloodless, dull and wintry sort of thing.
To the person who is just waiting for blossoms, I want to show spring in the grasses among the snow.
The grasses among the snow hold the quickening of spring itself.
This is not the dreary cold stillness of winter, but the stillness of light and warmth held within this wintry world.*
This is the experience of our zazen.
This is the experience of each moment, one after another: from the cold and wintry stillness your whole world becomes visible.
This is getting to zero.
It's like a blanket of snow.
You're not adding anything, you're not presupposing anything, you're not pushing away any difficulty, you're accepting everything, and so nothing is in the way.

Allow the experience of the shape of the bowls in your hands, the curve of the bare branches, the sound of the water, the full connection with your body, no matter what it feels, to express themselves.
Allow each part of your body, as you sit here, to sit zazen fully alert and engaged, functioning as itself, each thing inside as well as outside.
Meet it.
This is how we endeavor to practice on the cushion when we sit zazen, and when we move outside the gate, this precious opportunity to get to zero.
In conclusion, I'd like to ask you to take a moment to just reflect back on your intention for this practice period.
Maybe it's what came up last night in the warm open moment when you spoke.
Maybe there's something else in there that you're touching now as you're listening to this, and you've been sitting the morning of zazen and are touching something else.
Perhaps just take a moment to sit with that.
And I'd like to read you some suggestions for practices.
These again are modified from Sojin Roshi, with my own particular seasoning.
*What are you endeavoring to accomplish?
Be careful about your obligations while honoring your practice and commitment, balancing and integrating zazen in your daily activities.
This means creating a reasonable schedule without cherry picking the events.
You will most likely end up letting go of some minor activities of your life for the time in order to make your participation meaningful.
For most of us it's hard to add extra zazen, but if you can do it, do it, and don't pick and choose what you do.

If you make a commitment to yourself at the beginning of practice period and you say, I'm going to sit these days, Zoom zendo in the morning, here for the class on Monday and here on Thursday nights, do those things.
Sometimes emergencies come up, that's okay, but try and keep your commitments.
That's part of continuous practice.*
*It's not how you feel in the moment, it's what your intention is.
It's important to make an effort and pay attention to your home and work practice.
Ask for your family's support, let them know what you're doing.
Please try to come prepared to class and think about your questions.
We bring out the dharma together.
Here are some practices you can do anytime.
Patience.
Settle on the present moment and complete one activity before going to the next.
Use time intentionally.
Don't be pulled around by time, media, social media, the speed in which the world needlessly operates.
Whatever you choose to do, ask: is it necessary, is it the right time, is it helpful to me?*
*See what comes up.
Be aware of being centered.
Always know where your breath is and take time many times during the day to find it again and again.
Breathe from your hara.
Engage in each activity totally and thoroughly.
Make a practice of meeting people eye to eye and connecting, even for a second.
It's the relationship, not the process, even when you're busy, unless it's an emergency.
Be mindful of intention.
Without intentional practice there's no way to train, and it's difficult to sustain.
That intention is that deeper root.
That's where the nourishment comes from, from your own yearning, and the teacher and the shuso will be an inspiration.
They're a little extra fertilizer, but that's in you.
Be aware of it.
Consider choosing, for example, one step on the [unclear: "eighth world path"] we'll be studying and spend some time this practice period studying it.
Be the example too.
Your practice is a gift to each other.
Ask questions, questions are always welcome.*
What are your questions?
Yeah, I've managed to time this so that there is no time for questions, which was not intentional, but that's what happened.
So please support the shuso and enjoy the practice.
